soil-found-014.title: Soil pH, the number that runs soil chemistry
soil-found-014.text: On the pH scale, 3.5 and 9.5 look like near neighbors. In hydronium ions they are a millionfold apart. Soil pH measures how acidic or basic, also called alkaline, a soil is. Strictly, pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of hydronium ion activity, hydronium being the acid-carrying form of the hydrogen ion. Because the scale is logarithmic, a solution at pH 3.5 holds one million times more hydronium ions than one at pH 9.5. For soils, pH is read in a slurry with water or with a salt solution such as 0.01 M CaCl2. Values normally fall between 3 and 10, with 7 neutral. Ultra-acidic soils below pH 3.5 and very strongly alkaline soils above pH 9 are rare. Soil scientists call pH a master variable. It controls the chemical forms of nutrients and the reactions they undergo, and so what plants can take up. Most plants do best between pH 5.5 and 7.5, though many have adapted to thrive outside it. Most crops prefer pH 6.5 on mineral soils and 5.5 on organic soils. Highly acidic soils tend to hold toxic amounts of aluminum and manganese. Climate pushes pH both ways. In high-rainfall soils, hydronium ions displace basic cations, positively charged ions such as calcium, and the soil acidifies. In dry areas unleached calcium pushes pH to 8.5, and sodium held on the soil can raise it to 10. Where weathering is more advanced, pH is generally lower.

soil-found-001.title: Soil horizons, the layers that record a soil's life
soil-found-001.text: Cut down through a soil and you usually cross a series of bands. Each band is a horizon: a layer roughly parallel to the surface whose physical, chemical and biological traits differ from those above and below. Horizons are made by soil-forming processes. Layers those processes have not touched are simply called layers. Given time, an undifferentiated soil evolves a profile of two or more horizons. They differ greatly in thickness and generally lack sharp boundaries. Most are recognized by color and texture, described outright or relative to their neighbors, as coarser, sandier or darker. No profile has every major horizon, and some soils, such as soils described in {{ref:soil-class-094}}, have one horizon or none at all. Horizons are also fragile. Erosion can strip the upper ones and bury others downslope, and tillage, tree growth and major earthworks disturb or erase them. Going down a profile goes back in time. Pollen, testate amoebae and plant remains record past environmental change, and charcoal allows radiocarbon dating of a horizon. Most classification systems define soil types by horizons, either as whole sequences, as in the German system, or as selected diagnostic horizons. A shorthand of letters and numbers labels each one, recording color, texture, structure, consistency, roots, pH, voids, boundaries and nodules.

soil-found-024.title: Buffering: why some soils shrug off acid
soil-found-024.text: Add the same acid to two soils, and one barely budges while the other's pH plunges. The difference is buffering capacity, a soil's resistance to a change in pH when acid or basic material is added. It works through {{ref:soil-chem-047}} and neutralization, and carbonates also regulate pH. Different buffer systems take over at different pH, from calcium carbonate to iron. Pure sand has almost no buffering ability. Soils rich in fine mineral or organic particles, called colloids, buffer strongly. Within one kind of soil, buffering rises with {{ref:soil-chem-046}}. So clay- and humus-rich soils need more lime for the same change in pH. The reason is stored acidity. Lime must neutralize the acid cations held on colloids, not just the free acid in solution, or the stored cations restore the original pH. The lime needed depends on how finely it is ground and on buffering capacity. Once the colloids are saturated with hydronium, the buffer is spent, and further acid drives pH lower.

soil-found-025.title: Soil color, the first thing anyone notices
soil-found-025.text: Soils come brown, red, yellow, black, gray, white and even blue or green. Color is often a soil's most visually apparent property and the first impression it makes. It varies across landscapes, between horizons and even within a single clod. Color itself does not change how a soil behaves. It forms through chemical and biological weathering, especially the reactions described in {{ref:soil-chem-113}}. Elements released from the original minerals combine into new colored compounds. Ordinary conditions give uniform or gradual changes in color. Reducing environments, short of oxygen, produce disrupted, mottled patterns with points of concentrated color. Mineralogy is the main influence. Because color, especially its lightness, changes with moisture, it may be described both moist and dry. Sources disagree on what color is worth. One says it has little use in predicting soil characteristics. Another says it reveals soil organic matter, mineralogy, moisture and how much has been washed out.

soil-found-019.title: Aluminum, the hidden poison of acid soils
soil-found-019.text: Every soil contains aluminum, yet in most it does no harm. Aluminum toxicity is damage to plants from dissolved aluminum, and it is the most widespread problem of acid soils. The toxic form, the dissolved ion Al3+, is most soluble at low pH. Above pH 5.0 most soils hold little soluble aluminum. Roots show the damage first. Root tips and side roots thicken, fine branching is lost and the tips may turn brown. The poison then disrupts the uptake and transport of calcium and other nutrients, cell division, cell wall formation and enzyme activity. Acid soils add other stresses: hydrogen and manganese toxicity, and shortages of calcium and magnesium. Manganese symptoms appear below pH 5.6. Acid rain is the main force mobilizing aluminum from natural sources. The shift near pH 5 also marks a boundary in soil life, from acid-tolerant to acid-intolerant communities.

soil-found-018.title: What pushes a soil toward acid or alkaline
soil-found-018.text: Rain itself is slightly acidic. At an average pH of 5.6, from dissolved carbon dioxide, it washes basic cations out of soil and raises the share of aluminum and hydrogen ions. Many forces set a soil's pH, beginning with the minerals the soil formed from and the weathering they have undergone. In warm, humid climates soils acidify as weathering products wash away. In dry climates, weaker weathering and less washing leave soils neutral or alkaline. Life adds acid too. Respiration and decay release CO2, and roots release H+ ions when plants take up more cations than anions, the negatively charged ions. Ammonium fertilizers, acid rain and oxidizing sulfide minerals in mine spoil or {{ref:soil-chem-030}} acidify further. Alkalinity rises with minerals rich in sodium, calcium, magnesium and potassium, and with bicarbonate-rich irrigation water. Where too little water flows through, carbonates and bicarbonates build up. Soils rich in calcium carbonate range from pH 7.0 to 9.5, depending on whether calcium or sodium dominates.

soil-found-016.title: Reading pH from heather, litmus and glass electrodes
soil-found-016.text: A soil's pH can be read before any instrument comes out. The profile gives hints. A poorly mixed organic layer suggests strong acidity, a layer of {{ref:soil-chem-036}} alkaline conditions, and columnar structure sodic, or sodium-rich, conditions. Plants are clues too. Calcifuges, plants of acid soils, such as heathers, rhododendrons and gorse, mark acid ground. Calcicoles, lime-lovers such as ash, dogwoods and clematis, mark lime-rich ground. Cheap kits mix soil with an indicator solution that changes color. Litmus paper dipped in a soil–water mix turns red if the soil is acidic and blue if it is basic. Electronic meters insert an electrode into moist soil or a soil–water suspension and give a digital reading. Spectrophotometric methods, developed in the 2010s, add an indicator dye to a soil extract instead. They avoid the drift and suspension effects of glass electrodes. The USDA laboratory method mixes 20 g of soil with 20 mL of water and reads pH after standing 1 h. It then adds CaCl2 and reads pH again in 0.01 M CaCl2.

soil-found-020.title: How pH decides which nutrients plants can reach
soil-found-020.text: A soil can be full of nutrients and still starve a crop. Soil pH governs which ions are released or held, and so which nutrients plants can take up. Most minerals dissolve more readily in acid soils. Yet, trading toxicity against need, most nutrients are best available at moderate pH. Below pH 5.0, roots damaged by aluminum take up less, and deficiencies of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium and magnesium are frequent. Raising pH works unevenly. Molybdenum becomes more available, while zinc, iron, copper and manganese become less so. At high pH these trace nutrients move poorly, a deficit that water-soluble chelates, compounds that hold a metal in soluble form, can correct. Phosphorus was long thought most available near neutrality, at pH 6.5–7.5. Between pH 5.5 and 6.5, though, raising pH may increase, decrease or not affect it. In calcareous soils above 2% calcium carbonate, supplying phosphorus, iron, manganese, copper or zinc is often more efficient than trying to acidify.

soil-found-002.title: O, A, E, B, C, R: the alphabet of a soil profile
soil-found-002.text: Six capital letters, most commonly O, A, E, B, C and R, name the main layers of a soil profile. These are the master horizons. Many soils start with an organic surface layer, O. The mineral soil usually begins with an A horizon, the layer with the most organic matter and soil life. Below may lie an E horizon, a leached layer. A B horizon is a well-developed subsoil where substances moving down from the topsoil accumulate. A C horizon is loose but poorly developed material beneath. R is hard bedrock that cannot be dug by hand. Mature profiles typically have three basic master horizons, A, B and C, and the A and B together normally make up the solum. Suffixes of lowercase letters and figures split the master horizons further. Most systems define more horizons and layers than these, and the letters may differ. The USDA field book adds L for limnic, or lake-laid, materials, W for water and M for root-limiting manufactured layers. Because the systems define their symbols differently, they cannot be mixed, and none is more correct than another.

soil-found-023.title: Turning an alkaline soil more acid
soil-found-023.text: Sometimes the goal is a more acid soil. Lowering soil pH means adding acidifying agents or acidic organic materials to an alkaline soil. Elemental sulfur, 90–99% pure, is applied at 300–500 kg/ha and slowly oxidizes in the soil to sulfuric acid. Some fertilizers also work, because their ammonium oxidizes to nitric acid: ammonium sulfate, {{ref:soil-fert-071}} and {{ref:soil-fert-021}}. Sphagnum moss and the material described in {{ref:soil-class-070}} are acidifying organic additions. There is a limit. In high-pH soils with more than 2% calcium carbonate, acidifying is very costly and ineffective.

soil-found-017.title: Lime lovers and lime haters among plants
soil-found-017.text: Plants take sides on pH. Each species is adapted to its own range of soil pH. Calcifuges prefer acid soils and calcicoles lime-rich ones. Calcicole species outnumber calcifuges, so plant diversity tends to rise from pH 3.5 toward pH 9. Some ranges are narrow: Monterey pine grows at pH 4.5–5.2, while vetiver grass tolerates pH 3.0–8.0. The soil matters too. Soybeans may fail at pH 5.5 where molybdenum is low, yet grow optimally at that pH where it is sufficient. Breeders use differences between varieties to develop aluminum- and manganese-tolerant cereals for strongly acidic soils.

soil-found-022.title: Soil life and pH, each shaping the other
soil-found-022.text: pH shapes soil life, and soil life shapes pH. Microbes and animals respond to pH directly and through nutrient status, metal toxicity and the forms described in {{ref:soil-bio-095}}, so communities shift as pH changes. At low pH, aluminum causes oxidative stress that harms soft-bodied fauna without a hard outer skeleton: protists, nematodes, {{ref:soil-bio-087}} and earthworms. The traffic runs both ways. Many fungi acidify soil by excreting oxalic acid, which locks calcium into insoluble calcium oxalate crystals. Earthworm mucus, weakly alkaline at pH 7.5 to 8, buffers pH. Burrowing animals that mix organic and mineral matter reduce acidity, as in {{ref:soil-bio-096}}.

soil-found-021.title: When pH extremes leave plants thirsty
soil-found-021.text: A soil can hold water that plants still cannot use, and extreme pH is one reason. Strongly alkaline soils are sodic, rich in sodium, and dispersive, their particles drifting apart. Water soaks in slowly, moves through poorly and is stored badly. When wet, these soils are poorly aerated. When dry, they quickly lose plant-available water and turn hard and cloddy. Strongly acidic soils fail differently. Aluminum toxicity stunts roots so badly that plants run short of water even when the soil is relatively moist.

soil-found-015.title: From ultra acidic to very strongly alkaline: pH classes
soil-found-015.text: US soil surveyors give each stretch of the pH scale a name. The classes come from {{ref:soil-hist-050}}. On the acid side, ultra acidic is below 3.5, extremely acidic 3.5–4.4, very strongly acidic 4.5–5.0, strongly acidic 5.1–5.5, moderately acidic 5.6–6.0 and slightly acidic 6.1–6.5. Neutral is a band, not a point: pH 6.6–7.3. Above it, slightly alkaline is 7.4–7.8, moderately alkaline 7.9–8.4, strongly alkaline 8.5–9.0 and very strongly alkaline above 9.0.

soil-found-011.title: How Australia names its soil horizons
soil-found-011.text: The Australian Soil and Land Survey Field Handbook (2009) adds P and D horizons, drops E, and numbers sub-horizons of A and B. P horizons, named after peats, are organic layers formed in soil saturated with water, with 12 to 18% or more organic carbon depending on clay content. A splits into A1, dark and most biologically active, A2, paler, and A3, transitional to B. B splits into B1, B2 and B3. Leached layers are classed as A or B by their other properties. D marks material below the {{ref:soil-form-024}} that is unlike the layers above. As a rule of thumb, layers thinner than about 5 cm are described as pans or segregations within one horizon, and excessive subdivision is to be avoided.

soil-found-010.title: The international code for soil layers
soil-found-010.text: The manual of {{ref:soil-class-016}} sets out its horizon and layer symbols in Chapter 10 of its manual, 4th edition, published in 2022. It first separates organic layers, with at least 20% organic carbon, from organotechnic layers rich in artefacts, objects made by people, and from mineral layers. Its master symbols are H, O, A, E, B, C and R. I marks permanent layers of at least 75% ice, and W marks water. H layers are saturated for over 30 consecutive days in most years or have been drained; they are typically the material of {{ref:soil-class-070}}. O layers are not. Fine earth is the soil fraction of 2 mm or less. The soil surface is taken below any litter layer, which is over 90% recognizable dead plant tissue.

soil-found-026.title: Munsell charts: color as hue, value and chroma
soil-found-026.text: In a survey record, a Cecil soil horizon is not just red. It is red (10R 4/8) clay. That notation comes from the Munsell color system, which specifies a color by hue, value and chroma and is the standard way surveyors record soil color. Albert H. Munsell created the system early in the 20th century. The USDA adopted it for soil research in the 1930s, and the soil charts keep only the colors most relevant to soil. Hue is the dominant spectral color, in soil generally yellow or red. Charts conventionally show 40 hues in steps of 2.5, such as 10R to 2.5YR, and each page of the soil color book shows one hue. Value, lightness or darkness, increases from the bottom of the page to the top. Chroma, the intensity of color, increases from left to right, and a chroma of 0 is neutral gray, written N with a value, as in N 5/. Soil counts as moist when adding water no longer changes its color, and as dry when air-dried.

soil-found-027.title: What red, gray and black soils reveal
soil-found-027.text: Soil colors are a code for what happens underground. Read correctly, they reveal how much soil organic matter a soil holds, along with its iron chemistry, aeration and salts. Dark brown or black usually means plenty of soil organic matter, which coats mineral grains and darkens them. Accumulated charcoal also turns soil black. Sodium helps {{ref:soil-bio-089}} disperse and reach more minerals, so it influences how deep the dark color extends. Red signals iron that has accumulated or oxidized in oxygen-rich, well-aerated soil. Yellow also reflects iron, but in less oxygen-rich settings. Gray or blue marks saturated soil without oxygen, where iron has been reduced or depleted. Green can come from iron reduction or from minerals such as glauconite, melanterite and celadonite. White is common where salts, carbonates or calcite accumulate, often in arid environments, while jarosite can color acidic soils yellow. The {{ref:soil-form-010}} holds less of this dark material than the layer above. It takes its color mainly from iron oxides, usually brownish or reddish.

soil-found-028.title: Gleying: how waterlogged soil turns gray
soil-found-028.text: Waterlogged soil turns gray, and the reason is iron. Gleying is the development of gray or bluish, low-chroma colors in waterlogged soils as iron is reduced or removed. Without oxygen, microbes convert iron from the ferric form, Fe3+, to the ferrous form, Fe2+. Less often they reduce manganese from Mn4+ to Mn2+. Reduced iron is soluble. During prolonged saturation it can be carried away, exposing the light gray of bare silicate minerals. When the soil dries and oxygen returns, iron re-oxidizes locally into yellow-brown, reddish or orange mottles, often along root channels and burrows. Gleyed material can begin a few centimeters below the surface and continue almost unchanged for many meters.

openers.reading-a-soil: Dig a pit, and a soil starts to explain itself. Its layers lie roughly parallel to the surface, each different from the ones above and below, and the main ones carry capital letters, most commonly O, A, E, B, C and R. Its color is often the first thing anyone notices. Beneath the visible lies a chemical reading, how acidic or alkaline the soil is, set first by the minerals it formed from and the weathering they have undergone. That one measure governs which nutrients plants can reach, whether dissolved aluminum harms their roots, and which plants and soil organisms thrive there.

reviews.reading-a-soil: This chapter read a soil in two ways. By eye, its horizons follow a shared code of capital letters, though Australia and the international WRB scheme spell it differently, and its colors are recorded on Munsell charts: red for oxidized iron, black for organic matter, gray for the waterlogging that drives gleying. By chemistry, pH acts as a master variable that controls nutrient availability, sets the danger from dissolved aluminum and decides whether calcifuges or calcicoles take hold. Rain, roots, fertilizers and parent minerals push pH up or down, while buffering capacity resists them and decides how much lime a correction takes. Soil life both answers to pH and changes it, from acid-excreting fungi to earthworms whose mucus buffers it.
